subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If y = ax^(n+1) + bx^(−n), prove that x²y″ = n(n + 1)y.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.203, chapter 9 DIFFERENTIATION, Short Answer question 14. recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say which rule you use on each term and what you do after the second derivative.

steps.label: Differentiate term by term
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both terms are powers of x, so the power rule alone is enough — no product rule and no chain rule anywhere in this question.
lines: Differentiate each power by bringing the index down and reducing it by one:

recall.must_convey: That the power rule gives y′ = a(n + 1)xⁿ − bn x⁻ⁿ⁻¹.
accept: use the power rule on both terms
y dash is a into n plus one x to the n minus b n x to the minus n minus one
bring the index down and reduce it by one
power rule vaadali, index ni kinda ki techi one thagginchali
the second term keeps a minus sign because the index is negative

steps.why: The power rule applies to a negative index exactly as it does to a positive one, so both terms are handled by the same single rule.
common_mistakes: Writing the derivative of bx⁻ⁿ as bn x⁻ⁿ⁻¹ with a plus sign.
Reducing the index of x⁻ⁿ to x⁻ⁿ⁺¹ instead of x⁻ⁿ⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: Reducing an index by one always moves it DOWN the number line: −n becomes −n − 1, not −n + 1.

steps.label: Differentiate again
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both terms now carry the same factor n(n + 1) — that shared factor is the whole reason the result works.

recall.must_convey: That y″ = an(n + 1)xⁿ⁻¹ + bn(n + 1)x⁻ⁿ⁻², with n(n + 1) common to both terms.
accept: differentiate again and both terms carry n into n plus one
y double dash is a n n plus one x to the n minus one plus b n n plus one x to the minus n minus two
the two minus signs in the second term make it positive
rendo term lo rendu minus lu positive avuthai
n into n plus one is common to both terms
heard_as: x to the n minus one

steps.why: Multiplying by −n and then by −n − 1 gives +n(n + 1), so the second term turns positive and matches the first term’s factor.
common_mistakes: Keeping the second term negative by multiplying only one of the two minus signs.
Writing the index of the second term as −n − 1 instead of −n − 2.
steps.memory_tip: Two negatives multiply to a positive, which is why both terms end up with the same +n(n + 1).

steps.label: Multiply by x²
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Adding 2 to each index is the move the question is built on: n − 1 becomes n + 1 and −n − 2 becomes −n, the two indices y itself carries.

recall.must_convey: That multiplying by x² raises each index by 2, giving xⁿ⁺¹ and x⁻ⁿ.
accept: multiply by x squared and add two to each index
n minus one plus two is n plus one
minus n minus two plus two is minus n
x square tho multiply cheste index lo two add avuthundi
the indices become the same as in y

steps.why: Multiplying powers adds indices. Adding 2 restores exactly the two indices y started with, which is why the right-hand side can be written as a multiple of y.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the coefficients by 2 instead of adding 2 to the indices.
Applying x² to only the first term.
steps.memory_tip: Multiplying powers of x adds the indices; it never multiplies them.

steps.label: Take out n(n + 1)
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The bracket left behind must be y written out exactly as the question gives it — say so in words, or the proof is not finished.
lines: The bracket is y itself, so

recall.must_convey: That n(n + 1) is taken out and the remaining bracket is y, giving x²y″ = n(n + 1)y.
accept: take n into n plus one common and the bracket is y
the bracket is exactly the original y
so x squared y double dash is n into n plus one times y
n into n plus one common teeste bracket lo y vasthundi
that completes the proof

steps.why: A proof of this shape is finished only by naming the bracket as y. Stopping at the expanded line leaves the required statement unwritten.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the expanded form without saying the bracket is y.
Taking out n(n + 1) from one term only.
steps.memory_tip: Check with n = 1 and b = 0: y = ax², y″ = 2a, x²y″ = 2ax² = 1·2·y.

insider_note: Differentiate twice as plain powers; the second term's index −n − 1 times −n turns the sign positive. Multiplying by x² restores the original powers, so the bracket becomes y.
